abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Bioactive peptide therapeutics has been a long-standing research topic. Notably, the antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have been extensively studied for its therapeutic potential. Meanwhile, the demand for annotating other therapeutic peptides, such as antiviral peptides (AVPs) and anticancer peptides (ACPs), also witnessed an increase in recent years. However, we conceive that the structure of peptide chains and the intrinsic information between the amino acids is not fully investigated among the existing protocols. Therefore, we develop a new graph deep learning model, namely TP-LMMSG, which offers lightweight and easy-to-deploy advantages while improving the annotation performance in a generalizable manner. The results indicate that our model can accurately predict the properties of different peptides. The model surpasses the other state-of-the-art models on AMP, AVP and ACP prediction across multiple experimental validated datasets. Moreover, TP-LMMSG also addresses the challenges of time-consuming pre-processing in graph neural network frameworks. With its flexibility in integrating heterogeneous peptide features, our model can provide substantial impacts on the screening and discovery of therapeutic peptides. The source code is available at https://github.com/NanjunChen37/TP_LMMSG.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The discovery of peptide therapeutics has always been a focal point of drug development. Distinguished from small molecule drugs and biological agents, peptide drugs capture researchers’ attention by their unique advantages [1, 2]. In recent years, the progress in synthesis, modification, and analytical technologies have propelled therapeutic peptide research into a new era [2]. Concurrently, the continuous evolution of machine learning models has played a pivotal role in accelerating the peptide drug discovery pipeline. Alongside the widely acknowledged antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) prediction models, the field has witnessed the successive emergence of antiviral peptides (AVPs) and anticancer peptides (ACPs) prediction models [3–5]. The AMPs have attracted widespread attention due to their broad-spectrum antibacterial activity [6, 7]. Specifically, AMPs belongs to a class of short peptides (around 6 to 100 amino acids) involved in the innate immune response among lives [8, 9]. The general therapeutic mechanism of AMPs is to bind the surface of microorganisms through the attraction effect between positive and negative charges. Specifically, most AMPs have net-positive charge, while bacterial membrane has negative charge. The interaction can directly or indirectly destroy the integrity of microbial membrane, thereby affecting the life cycle and proliferation of the microorganism [10, 11]. Moreover, evidence also suggests that the 3D structure of AMPs may also affect the antimicrobial activity of peptides [12, 13]. In addition to natural AMPs, it has been proven promising to discover new synthetic AMPs using generative models and synthetic workflows [14, 15]. Different from small molecules, peptide therapies mainly take advantage of higher specificity and lower toxicity. Hence, peptide drugs with specific targets are also adapted as antifungal, antiviral, antiparasitic or even anticancer clinical strategies [8, 16, 17].

To meet the increasing demand for model training and high-throughput screening of bioactive peptides, various public databases have been established. These databases provide different types of peptide information, allowing researchers to design machine learning models based on different objectives. The APD3 [9], dbAMP [18] and DRAMP [19] databases collect available AMP data and classify those AMPs into different categories based on their targets. Moreover, the experimental data and derived data, such as inhibition activity and molecular properties, are also included in these databases. Meanwhile, the databases such as CAMP [20], ADAM [21] and SATPdb [22] provide abundant peptide structural information. In 2021, several experimentally validated datasets were investigated [3], including APD3 [9], CAMP [20], dbAMP [18], DRAMP [19], LAMP [23] and YADAMP [24]. Based on the AMPs records in these datasets, a fusion dataset named XUAMP is constructed to thoroughly evaluate the performance of AMP identification models [3]. Meanwhile, the CD-HIT tool is utilized for rigorous sequence filtering and sampling to construct the independent test dataset [3]. The following model evaluations demonstrate that there is a potential for further enhancement in current AMP prediction models. In addition to AMPs, the APD3, CAMP, DRAMP and LAMP databases also contain diverse peptide information, including AVPs, ACPs and other theraputic peptides that target at different diseases.

Benefit from the peptide information in the aforementioned datasets, multiple feature representation approaches have also been proposed. Besides the commonly used one-hot encoding and multiple sequence alignment (MSA) encoding, incorporating amino acid physicochemical properties can also effectively improve model performance [25, 26]. Meanwhile, the use of positional encoding, amino acid composition and pseudo amino acid composition features was shown to enhance the model performance by incorporating detailed composition information of amino acids [25, 27, 28]. As for the prediction models, the random forest model amPEPpy demonstrates good predictive performance in distinguishing AMPs [29]. Recently, there has been an increasing trend in utilizing deep learning frameworks to distinguish AMPs and non-AMPs [30, 31]. Besides the composition features, the recently published AMPpred-MFA model incorporates dipeptide and k-mer composition as additional input features. Although these methods combine the position, composition and physicochemical properties of peptides, they do not leverage the structural information of the peptide. To tackle this, the sAMPpred-GAT model has been proposed. The model utilizes the protein structure predicted by trRosetta for AMP identification [32, 33]. Except for AMP prediction, some works have transferred the successful experience of predicting AMPs to other types of peptide identification tasks, and have developed prediction models specifically for AVP and ACP [4, 5]. Although sAMPpred-GAT is a promising and innovative attempt, there are still limitations in its practical application. First, the model only utilizes one-hot encoding, positional encoding, hidden Markov models (HMMs) encoding and position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM) encoding as the node features. Two of these features (HMM and PSSM) solely rely on MSA and protein sequence databases [34, 35]. This indicates that the model lacks explicit representations of amino acid physicochemical properties. The two rounds of MSA also implies that the bottleneck in the model’s runtime lies in the feature extraction stage (e.g. around 15 s on single sample). Additionally, its complete deployment requires the download of the entire nonredundant protein sequence database (nrdb, 0.5 TB). Therefore, it is crucial to improve the effectiveness and storage occupancy of the model.

In this study, we aim to develop a peptide prediction model, which not only predicts AMPs, but also generalizes to predict other types of peptides (i.e. AVPs and ACPs). Moreover, we aim to reduce the storage occupancy and feature encoding time in graph neural network applications. So far, protein embeddings have been demonstrated to be successful at both sequence and amino acid levels [36, 37]. Meanwhile, the hierarchical multi-scale residual network (HMSRN) has been proved promising in protein–RNA interaction prediction tasks [38]. Therefore, we adapt multiple pre-trained language models to obtain the amino acid embeddings. The HMSRN is then applied to extract informative features among the language model embeddings. Subsequently, we concatenate the extracted features into each node of peptide graph for graph learning. We name our approach as the Therapeutic Peptide Language Model Multi-Scale Graph neural network (TP-LMMSG). The experimental results reveal that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models in multiple evaluation metrics. Remarkably, these achievements are attained without employing HMM features and rely solely on the lightweight nonredundant protein sequence database 90 (nrdb90) [39]. In addition to AMP prediction, we further generalize our model to the prediction tasks of AVPs and ACPs. Our model also exhibits remarkable performance, surpassing existing models in identifying the other types of peptides with imbalanced datasets.

sec.title: Datasets
sec.p: To ensure a fair evaluation and enable an objective comparison with previously proposed models, we primarily utilize the seven AMP datasets provided in previous literatures (i.e. XUAMP, APD3, CAMP, dbAMP, DRAMP, LAMP and YADAMP [3, 9, 18–20, 23, 24, 32]). Specifically, the XUAMP dataset is integrated from multiple datasets including APD3, DRAMP, LAMP, CAMP, dbAMP and YADAMP, resulting in 5536 AMPs/nonAMPs in the training set, and 1536 AMPs/nonAMPs in the independent test set. We choose to benchmark on this dataset as the primary evaluation. Besides the XUAMP dataset, we also conduct evaluations on the other six datasets mentioned above (Table 1, Figure S1). Specifically, each independent test dataset of the six datasets has undergone strict filtering rules, where CD-HIT tool is applied to ensure no sequence shares more than 40% identity in the test set [3, 40, 41]. In this manner, we can rigorously evaluate the performance and make a thorough comparison with previously proposed methods. As for the AVPs and ACPs datasets, the number of positive samples is considerably fewer than that for AMPs [17]. To ensure a fair comparison, we adapt the dataset utilized in previous publications, which are FFMAP AVPs dataset and ACP-ML ACPs dataset, respectively (Table 1) [4, 5].

sec.title: The overview of TP-LMMSG model
sec.p: The architecture of TP-LMMSG consists of five parts (Figure 1). Firstly, the predictive amino acids connectivity is obtained with trRosetta to construct basic peptide graph (Figure 1A). Secondly, the basic amino acid level features are extracted by conducting one-hot encoding, position encoding, PSI-BLAST and HHBlits on peptide sequences. We consider the lightweight graph construction method, where running HHBlits is optional (the portions with dash lines in Figure 1A). These features are assigned as the initial graph node features (Figure 1B). For the third step, the SeqVec and ProtTrans pre-trained protein language models are used to obtain the amino acids level embeddings, including the hidden representation of hydrophilia, electrical properties and polarity [36, 37]. Specifically, the pretrained SeqVec model and PortTrans model are adapted to extract the biophysical embeddings of each amino acid in the peptide sequence [36, 37]. For the output of each pre-trained model, an HMSRN is utilized to extract the physicochemical information at different scales (Figure 1C). In the last two steps, the latent representation is integrated for each amino acid in the peptide graph (Figure 1D). A graph attention network (GAT) followed by fully connected layers is proposed to predict whether the input peptides are positive samples or negative samples (Figure 1E).

sec.title: Connectivity prediction and basic feature encoding
Protein language model based embeddings extraction
Flexible HMSRN
sec.p: After obtaining the amino acid level embeddings, we adapt the HMSRN architecture to extract features at the amino acid level (Figure 1C). The aim of utilizing the HMSRN is to capture node features comprehensively while alleviating the gradient vanishing problem [44]. In this work, the HMSRN is optimized to receive a varying number of language model embeddings and conduct feature concatenation at the amino acid level.

sec.p: The evaluation metrics used in this work are listed in equation 15. These metrics allow us to objectively compare the performance of our model with the SOTA models. For the imbalanced datasets ACP and AVP, we also compute the Area Under the Precision-Recall (AUPR) curve.

sec.title: Performance comparison with other methods
sec.p: We first compare the predictive performance of both the lightweight and heavyweight model with the other 13 methods. The frequently adopted models for performance comparison include AMPscannerV2, iAMP-2L, ADAM-SVM/HMM, ampir, MLAMP, AMPlify, AMPEP, AMPfun and AMPpred-EL, which are comprehensively evaluated in the previous studies [3, 45]. We further replicate other SOTA AMP prediction models, including amPEPpy, AMPpred-MFA and sAMPpred-GAT. We follow the data processing protocols in the previous benchmark experiments to avoid bias [3, 32].

caption.p: The performance comparison of TP-LMMGS with the other 13 AMP prediction models on XUAMP test set

fn.p: Note: All results generated in this study are obtained from 10 repetitions with random model initialization. The bold and underlined data refer to the best and second best value of each evaluation metric.

sec.p: Besides the XUAMP dataset, our model on the remaining six datasets constantly exhibits promising performance (Figure 2). Given no significant difference observed between sAMPpred-GAT(full_nrdb) and sAMPpred-GAT(nrdb90), we adopt the latter for subsequent evaluations. The box plots reveal that our model outperforms the previous methods on every dataset. By strictly following the feature extraction procedure of the amPEPpy approach, we find that the amPEPpy model exhibits a similar AUC score on the APD3 dataset compared with AMPpred-MFA and sAMPpred-GAT. However, the amPEPpy model struggles with performance bias on several datasets, including dbAMP, DRAMP and LAMP. Nevertheless, our approaches demonstrate stable performance advantages across multiple datasets, highlighting the robustness of our method across diverse AMP data. The detailed evaluation metrics tables of model performance on the six datasets are listed in Tables S2–S5.

caption.p: Performance comparison among the amPEPpy, AMPpred-MFA, sAMPpred-GAT and two versions of TP-LMMSG models on seven AMP independent test sets. All results generated in this study are obtained from 10 repetitions with random model initialization.

sec.title: Model interpretation with t-SNE
sec.p: In this section, we analyze the differences in feature extraction among the three deep learning approaches: AMPpred-MFA, sAMPpred-GAT (nrdb90) and TP-LMMSG (no_HMM). The learned features from the fully connected layer preceding the classification layer of each model are extracted and projected into 2D views (Figure 3 and Figure S3).

caption.p: The t-SNE visualization of deep learning models on XUAMP dataset. From left to right is AMPpred-MFA, sAMPpred-GAT, TP-LMMSG and raw language model output embedding.

sec.p: Through a horizontal comparison of the above three methods on seven datasets, the two methods with graph neural networks share similar feature distributions. On the other hand, the method AMPpred-MFA with LSTM layer separate the samples in a different manner. Compared with the other methods, TP-LMMSG illustrates a more uniform feature separation through all seven datasets. The positive samples’ feature projection demonstrates a higher level of concentration in the feature space. Moreover, the TP-LMMSG model also exhibits a remarkable separation in the border region between positive and negative samples. As for the AMPpred-MFA model, the decision boundary of the positive and negative samples are not clear. The sAMPpred-GAT model demonstrates superior performance compared with the AMPpred-MFA model, while still encounters similar challenges. However, for TP-LMMSG model, the incorporation of abundant node-level information help alleviate this issue. The t-SNE visualization of TP-LMMSG could provide insights into the enhanced positive sample prediction during previous evaluations.

In addition to the three deep learning model, the raw language model embeddings is also projected onto the 2D views. It appears that the embeddings of the language model exhibit a certain degree of discrimination between positive and negative samples. Specifically, LM embeddings demonstrate a more concentrated distribution for negative samples, while the embeddings of positive samples appear to be scattered in the feature space.

sec.title: Ablation analysis
sec.p: To further investigate how LM embeddings intrinsically influence our model, we aim to assess the impact of different features for peptide prediction. To achieve this, we conduct ablation experiments to examine the effect of each language model embedding. Specifically, for the four different pre-trained language models involved in this study, we first evaluate the effect of SeqVec embeddings. The amino acid level feature generated by ‘uni’, ‘bfd’ and ‘brt’ is subsequently incorporated into the model, resulting in a total of nine different feature combinations (Figure 4A). For each feature setting, we have also examined the influence of removing HMM features. A 10-fold cross-validation is conducted on the XUAMP dataset for objective evaluation with each feature combination (Figure S4).

caption.p: The result of ablation experiment, 10-fold cross-validation and time comparison. (A) The ablation experiment results for TP-LMMSG (HMM) and TP-LMMSG (no_HMM) with different LM feature. (B) The LM embedding correlation before and after the flexible HMSRN module.

sec.p: According to the radar chart of AUC and accuracy score, incorporating the language model generated feature indeed improves the overall performance of our model. With an increasing number of incorporated language models, there is a progressive enhancement in the model’s performance. Due to the absence of HMM features, when incorporating only up to two language model features, TP-LMMSG (no_HMM) exhibits lower accuracy and AUC score compared with TP-LMMSG (HMM). However, as more features are introduced, the impact of HMM features becomes less pronounced. The best performance of TP-LMMSG (no_HMM) is achieved when incorporating all four LM embeddings. Furthermore, we observe that the use of different language model features also has an impact on the model’s performance. The combination of ‘uni-bfd’ and ‘uni-brt’ features yield better results compare to the ‘bfd-brt’ combination. Specifically, the decreasing performance of ‘uni-brt’ and ‘bfd-brt’ compared with ‘uni-bfd’ has demonstrated the importance of the ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 generated feature to our model.

Besides the ablation cross-validation, we extracted the original language model embeddings and the HMSRN output features to investigate the effectiveness of HMSRN in extracting peptide features. We randomly sample 10% of peptide sequences among all positive and negative samples. The feature correlation between each sequence is then computed and visualized with heat maps (Figure 4B). According to the heat map, the first half of the X and Y axes represent the positive samples, while the second half represents the negative samples. It can be observed that the initial LM embeddings do not exhibit significant feature correlation. Only a slight correlation can be observed among the negative samples. However, the HMSRN output illustrates an obvious correlation pattern before merging with the peptide graph nodes. These results further support the improved positive sample detection of TP-LMMSG model.

sec.title: Time consumption comparisons
sec.p: In this section, we assess the advantages of our model in pre-processing compared with the previous sAMPpred-GAT method. In light of the variations in total sample sizes and sequence lengths across different datasets, we compare the pre-processing time of TP-LMMSG and sAMPpred-GAT on four different datasets, which are XUAMP, APD3, CAMP and dbAMP. The average duration is then calculated for comparison. The time comparison is carried on a Intel Core 13700K CPU (Figure S5). The average pre-processing time for sAMPpred-GAT based on dataset XUAMP, APD3, CAMP and dbAMP are 15.1, 15.0, 15.2 and 15.1 s, respectively. In contrast, by eliminating HMM encoding, our method can compress the average feature acquisition duration into around 2 s. Specifically, for each sample in the four datasets, the time consumption is 2.1, 2.0, 2.2 and 2.2 s, respectively. This result demonstrates that our model can learn sequence features within a reasonable duration, thus improving the applicability of graph neural networks in predicting peptide properties.

sec.title: Generalization ability assessment on AVP and ACP prediction tasks
sec.p: Through the previous experiments, we have validated the effectiveness of the TP-LMMSG model in AMP prediction. Moreover, the model has exhibited robustness when applied to different independent test datasets. Hence, we aim to generalize the model to other therapeutic peptide prediction tasks to further evaluate the generalization ability of our model. The two tasks involved in this section are AVPs prediction and ACPs prediction. We employ the AVP dataset and the ACP dataset provided in previous literature [4, 5]. Different from the AMP dataset, the AVPs and ACPs dataset are both imbalanced. The sample distribution is listed in Table 1 and Figure 5. We conduct a new round of training for the TP-LMMSG model based on those two datasets. The model’s performance on each dataset is evaluated through 10-fold cross-validation.

caption.p: The distribution of peptide sequence and sequence length of the independent test datasets for the AVP dataset and ACP datset.

sec.p: According to the result of AVP prediction, the TP-LMMSG model demonstrates an advantage over existing classification models (Table 3). It is worth noting that the previously proposed models only exhibit advantages across certain evaluation metrics. For example, the ENNAVIA model shows a higher accuracy, MCC and Sn score, while the AVPIden model exhibits a better AUC and AUPR score. The recently published FFMAVP model has the best Sp, while its other metrics are lower than the previous models. Nevertheless, the TP-LMMSG model achieves superiority across all metrics in the AVP prediction task. Compared with the existing models, the TP-LMMSG model demonstrates over 3% higher accuracy, AUC, Sn and Sp. Moreover, the MCC score is observed for an increase of 5%. The high AUPR values further suggest that our model exhibits strong performance even in the presence of imbalanced data.

caption.p: The performance comparison among TP-LMMSG with the other three AVP prediction model

fn.p: Note: Results generated in this study are obtained with 10-fold cross-validation. The bold data refer to the best value of each evaluation metric.

sec.p: In the ACP prediction tasks, the TP-LMMSG model also demonstrated its superiority (Table 4). In the independent test sets, TP-LMMSG outperforms the existing SOTA models in terms of metrics of interest: accuracy (2.3%), AUC (1.1%), MCC (5.8%) and Sp (7.3%). In contrast to the previous AMP datasets, the AVP and ACP datasets have sequence lengths ranging from 7 to 121 and 5 to 255, respectively. It demonstrates that our prediction model exhibits robust generalization across datasets with diverse distributions of sequence lengths.

sec.p: Given the fact that positive and negative samples of therapeutic peptides show highly imbalanced distribution in the real world, we conduct a series of experiments on the XUAMP dataset with shrinking ratios of positive samples in the training dataset, thus to discover the performance boundary of peptide prediction models (Figure S6). Despite a noticeable decrease in the models’ predictive performance when the positive samples in training set are decreased to a proportion of 10%, TP-LMMSG still demonstrates reliable predictive performance compared with the other methods. Considering that the positive-to-negative sample ratios of AVP and ACP training datasets are approximately 0.27 and 0.33 respectively, TP-LMMSG continues to showcase its performance within this range.

sec.title: Discussion and conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we develop a new model that resolves the time-consuming pre-processing challenge encountered by previous graph neural network models. Meanwhile, our model outperforms the current SOTA AMP prediction models across all datasets. Additionally, the TP-LMMSG also demonstrates robustness on imbalanced datasets, surpassing the current SOTA AVP and ACP prediction models.

Previous studies have primarily relied on MSA and various amino acid properties as the feature representation [3, 36]. The residue features, k-mer features and overall characteristics of peptide sequences can be obtained from sequences, thus facilitating the peptide property prediction. On the other hand, graph neural networks can leverage structural information of peptide molecules, but face challenges in specific amino acid property feature representations. Moreover, due to the limited number of homologs for partial peptides, running MSA may not yield any informative sequence information. In practice, neither nrdb90 nor entire nrdb guarantees completed MSA results for all sequences. This may introduce biases in feature extraction. With the node-level language model embeddings, our model can incorporate a large number of amino acid property representations, making it possible to integrate amino acid property features into a graph neural network.

In addition, the optimization in pre-processing stage enables the practical application of graph neural networks for peptide property prediction tasks. Compared with the previous graph learning model, our approach achieves a pre-processing time reduction of over 7 folds. Therefore, even when applied to larger databases with fine-tuning, our approach yields highly accurate results within reasonable time-frames. Moreover, our method could save a large amount of local storage space, enabling efficient local fine-tuning and adaptation to hardware resources at the small-scale laboratory level.

The good performance and potential exhibited by the TP-LMMSG model have sparked deeper thinking for peptide property prediction. It is acknowledged that the distribution of therapeutic peptides with clinical potential is extremely imbalanced compared with negative samples in the real world. Our experimental results also explore the performance boundary. This series of experiments with imbalanced datasets demonstrates the robustness of TP-LMMSG. It also suggests that the continuous supplements of novel positive samples should be enabled and included in benchmark datasets to reflect the practical application context.

Taking it a step further, with the advancement of biosynthetic technology, the introduction of non-natural amino acids is emerging in peptide drug design [46]. In the future, peptide graphs that involve non-natural amino acids can be constructed through site-directed mutagenesis and the incorporation of distinct node and edge features. By utilizing Density Functional Theory derived features or traditional small molecule representations, the limitations of protein language models could be expanded in peptide prediction tasks [47]. These avenues hold promise for further investigation. Moreover, mounting evidence suggests that covalently attached small molecules to peptides demonstrate potential drug-like properties, posing challenges in molecule-peptide graph constructions [48, 49]. Fortunately, with the development of protein prediction models, AlphaFold3 has acquired the capability to predict drug–protein interaction poses, enhancing the expansion possibilities of our workflow [50]. While AlphaFold3 is not open-sourced during the writing of this article, exploring cutting-edge protein structure prediction models provides a valuable focus for peptide property annotations in the future.

list-item.p: A generalizable peptide prediction model, TP-LMMSG, is proposed. It outperforms current state-of-the-art models in antimicrobial peptides, antiviral peptides, and anticancer peptides predictions.
TP-LMMSG effectively tackles the challenge faced by previous graph neural network-based methods, which is the inability to extract and represent amino acid level properties.
The model utilizes optimized amino acid level feature extraction strategy for rapid deployment of graph neural networks in peptide prediction.
TP-LMMGS can flexibly incorporate novel language model embeddings. The architecture could providing continuous contributions to the discovery process of potential peptide therapeutics.
